label: explain-bm-making
one_line: We plan to print two-layer plastic strips that curl when damp, and first measure how much the plastic swells.
what: We want to make a thin strip from two layers of 3D-printed plastic. One layer swells when it gets wet. The other layer hardly swells. So the strip bends, like a leaf curling as it dries. A written rule says how far such a strip can bend. The rule depends on how much the wet layer grows and on how thick the strip is. We have drawn up five things to print, from one small strip to a small window-shade module. Before any of that, we must soak small test strips and measure how much each plastic swells. Nobody has published that number for these plastics.
why: Buildings use motors and sensors to open and close shades. A shade that moves by itself with the damp in the air would need no power. A rule that predicts the bend lets a designer plan such a part before printing it. First we must learn whether the rule holds for cheap, common printer plastics. Today the swelling of these plastics in damp air is not measured, so every prediction rests on one data sheet. We do not know yet if the idea works. The first test is small and costs about a thousand dollars in materials, if the lab borrows the big machines.

steps.text: Print flat test strips from several Formlabs plastics. The Form 4 printer holds one plastic at a time, so each plastic is a separate print.
steps.picture: Like baking one flavour of cookie per tray.

steps.text: Rinse the strips in alcohol, dry them, and bake them under light. Weigh them again and again until they stop getting lighter.
steps.picture: Like weighing laundry until it stops getting lighter.

steps.text: Measure each strip's length and thickness before it gets wet. Use a fixed camera with a ruler in the picture.
steps.picture: Like marking a child's height on a door frame, always from the same spot.

steps.text: Soak the strips in water and weigh them at set times. Weigh with a fine scale and a fixed wiping routine, because a thin film of water on the surface can weigh as much as the water inside.
steps.picture: Like weighing a sponge: squeeze the same way each time.

steps.text: Measure the length again after soaking. The change in length, about two parts in a thousand on a 40 millimetre strip, is less than the width of a hair.
steps.picture: A strip as long as a pencil stub that grows by less than a hair's width.

steps.text: Glue or print a swelling layer onto a layer that hardly swells, and note the thickness of each.
steps.picture: Like pressing a damp paper towel onto a dry plastic ruler.

steps.text: Wet the two-layer strip and photograph its curl from the side. Fit a circle to the curve to get the bend.
steps.picture: Like tracing a round plate to find its size.

steps.text: Compare the measured bend with the bend the written rule predicts from the swelling numbers.
steps.picture: Like checking a recipe's promised cooking time against your oven.

wrong_if: Our bet, written before we look: a strip with measured layer swelling and thickness will curl to within a fifth of the bend the rule predicts. For the first strip the prediction is a curl of about 41 millimetres radius, with a likely range of 28 to 83. If the curl is far outside that range, or if the plastic swells too little to see, we are wrong.
could_go_wrong: The swelling numbers come from one data sheet, and it does not say how thick the tested slab was.
The plastics may swell much less in damp air than in liquid water, so the strips may barely bend.
The two layers may not stick to each other well, and nobody has measured that bond.
Alcohol left inside a strip after rinsing could be mistaken for swelling in water.
The signal is tiny, about 80 micrometres on a 40 millimetre strip, so a cheap ruler or caliper cannot measure it.
The rule assumes a perfect bond and small bends, and the real strip may break those assumptions.
Thick layers soak slowly, so a metre-wide shade could need months to finish bending.
The plastic's stiffness when wet was estimated, not measured, and that may shift the predicted bend.

questions.q: How do you know the bend rule is right?
questions.a: We re-ran the project's check script and an independent solver. They agree to about one part in a billion. That shows the maths is consistent. It does not show real plastic obeys it.

questions.q: How do you know these plastics swell at all?
questions.a: One data sheet for Flexible 80A V2 says it gains 8 percent in mass and 3 percent in volume in one day in water. Other Formlabs plastics gain under 1 percent in their cube test, though one older soft one gains 2.3 percent.

questions.q: Has anyone built a damp-air bending part from printed resin before?
questions.a: Yes, partly. A 2024 paper printed a polyurethane ink that folds in under one second in humid air. It is not a Formlabs plastic and has no bend rule check. We found no part checked against a proof-assistant-checked law, but that is a search result, not proof.

questions.q: Why is the swelling so hard to measure?
questions.a: The change is tiny and the surface water confuses scales. It needs a fine scale, a fixed camera and a fixed routine.

questions.q: Would alcohol work better than water?
questions.a: Alcohol makes the soft plastic gain about 39 percent in a day, against under 0.1 percent for a hard one. That is far stronger, but the strips would stretch too much for the simple rule.

questions.q: Can I repeat this at home?
questions.a: Partly. A phone and kitchen scale can show whether a strip curls. They cannot give numbers good enough to test the rule. Proper kit costs one to two thousand dollars, or more if bought new.
We have not printed or soaked any strip. We have not measured swelling in damp air, bond strength, or wet stiffness. Several prices came from search snippets only.
A 0.4 millimetre layer would settle in hours to about a day. A louver blade might take 1 to 10 days. Both rest on an assumed slab thickness.

Softer rubber-like Formlabs resins, used here as the layer that hardly swells.

Hard Formlabs resins that swell very little.
A strip made of two stuck-together layers that react differently, so it bends.
To grow in size by soaking up liquid.

Air holding a lot of water vapour.
How tightly a strip curves; a small radius means a tight curl.
The distance from the centre of a circle to its edge, here used to describe a curl.
A formula from Timoshenko in 1925 that predicts how far a two-layer strip bends.

One thousandth of a millimetre; a human hair is about 70 of them wide.
How much matter something holds, which is what a scale reads.
How much space something takes up.

Isopropanol, a rubbing alcohol used to rinse printed parts.
A hand tool that measures length to about a fortieth of a millimetre.
A device that weighs things; a fine one reads to a ten-thousandth of a gram.

How hard a material pushes back when you bend or stretch it.
How well two layers stick to each other.
Software that checks a mathematical argument step by step.
A slanted slat in a window shade.
A soft, water-filled plastic that swells a lot.

check_yourself.what: Open the Flexible 80A V2 data sheet, page 6, and find the Deionized Water row.
check_yourself.expect: 1 day: +8 percent mass, +3 percent volume. 1 week: +9 percent mass, +7 percent volume.

check_yourself.what: Re-run the project's bend-limit check, which only reads files.
check_yourself.expect: Last line: VERDICT: the ceiling holds in every check; grid maximum 1.499998 at m^2 n = 0.99996

check_yourself.what: Recompute the instrument needs for the strips.
check_yourself.expect: Flexible 80A V2 strip 174.4 mg; 0.1 mg balance relative error 0.3 % at 8 % uptake; 80 um and 4.0 um length targets

check_yourself.what: Re-run all bend models and the seeded random trials.
check_yourself.expect: Object 1 pair A R_final median 41.0 mm, 5th to 95th 27.6 to 83.3 mm; curvature t90 0.719 and t99 1.653

left_out: Claim that no design checked by a proof assistant exists anywhere: left out as fact, because it is a search absence the verifier did not test (kept only as a hedged search result).
Claim that humidity actuators are slow and weak compared with heat-driven ones: left out as fact, only partly supported and a judgement; the 2024 film folds in under 1 second.
Claim that all Form 4 resins are acrylates and that no bond data exists: left out, because only 14 safety sheets were checked and the rest is a negative.
Claim that Flexible 80A V2 is the only resin that swells much: left out, because the older Elastic 50A V1 gains 2.3 percent in water.
Claim that no measurement of humid-air swelling exists at all: left out as fact, since sources cannot prove a negative; we only say we found none.
Claim that the Open Material Mode price of 3748.50 dollars was wrong: left out, because the earlier file was not read; only the 875 dollar per-printer price is confirmed and it is not used above.
Claim that the best pairs reach 99 percent of the bend limit and stiff pairs lose 41 to 89 percent: left out, because it rests on guessed stiffness values.
Exact diffusion speed and settling times: used only as hedged ranges, because they assume a 2 mm slab the data sheet never states.
